newsitem.title: USA: Drug kingpin given life in prison, no parole.
newsitem.headline: Drug kingpin given life in prison, no parole.

text.p: A U.S. judge on Friday sentenced drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego to life in prison without parole and ordered him to pay close to half a billion dollars in fines and forfeitures.

Garcia Abrego, 52, received a total of 11 life sentences and nine 20-year sentences, all to be served concurrently. He was convicted in October on charges of drug-trafficking, money laundering and bribery by a Houston federal jury.
In addition, U.S. District Judge Ewing Werlein fined Garcia Abrego $128 million and ordered him to forfeit $350 million in illicit proceeds.

Before his capture in January 1996 in the northern Mexico city of Monterrey, Garcia Abrego was one of the world's biggest drug traffickers and had been placed on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list. His Gulf cartel shipped billions of dollars of cocaine and marijuana to the United States starting in the 1970s, drug agents said.
Prosecutor Melissa Annis said the conviction and sentencing of Garcia Abrego was a death blow for the Gulf cartel. "If it's not dead, it's certainly mortally wounded," she told reporters.
Garcia Abrego showed little reaction when the stiff sentence was handed down. Standing before Werlein, he responded firmly, "No, senor," when the judge asked him if he had anything to say.
During the October trial, former cartel insiders testified that Garcia Abrego paid out millions of dollars in bribes to officials in Mexico and, to a lesser extent, the United States.

News reports have linked him to Raul Salinas, the brother of former Mexico President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, and high-level political assassinations in Mexico, but no ties have ever been confirmed.
Raul Salinas is in jail in Mexico City on charges that he ordered the 1994 killing of a ruling party official and that he illegally enriched himself during his brother's six-year term as president.

Despite much speculation that Garcia Abrego would try to strike a deal with prosecutors to give information in exchange for a lighter sentence, both Annis and defence attorney Tony Canales said it had not been discussed.

"We have never talked about that. Never, ever, ever, ever, ever," Canales said after the sentencing. He said he intended to appeal the October verdict and would base it partly on the government's use of convicted cartel insiders who were given lighter sentences in exchange for testimony against their former boss.

Garcia Abrego had been pursued by U.S. and Mexican drug agents for years, but eluded capture through guile and payoffs of law enforcement authorities in Mexico. A former cookie factory worker who was born in south Texas, he compiled a fortune that was estimated at $15 billion and included ranches and other properties throughout Mexico.
He was finally captured Jan. 14 by Mexican agents and flown two days later to Houston for trial on U.S. indictments.

Witnesses in his trial told of how he had built a vast empire that stretched from his base in northern Mexico to locations throughout the United States. They said he shipped cocaine from the Cali cartel in Colombia in exchange for half the profits.
Throughout it all, Garcia Abrego maintained his innocence and said he was not the head of the Gulf cartel. He did not testify in the trial.
Another defence attorney Mike Ramsey said it would be difficult for the United States to collect the money that Werlein ordered Garcia Abrego to pay because his property is mostly in Mexico.
"I guess there's some possibility the U.S. could realise the money, although I'd be shocked," he said.
